final_answer:
Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that works by recursively splitting the input into smaller subarrays until each subarray contains a single element. These single-element subarrays are inherently sorted. The algorithm then merges these subarrays back together in a sorted manner. The merging process involves comparing the first elements of each subarray and appending the smaller element to a new array, continuing this until all elements are merged. This process ensures the entire array is sorted.

Merge sort is preferred over quicksort for linked lists because it does not rely on random access to elements, which is inefficient in linked lists. Quicksort requires partitioning the list around a pivot, which is difficult to implement efficiently in linked lists due to their sequential access nature. Merge sort, on the other hand, can be implemented with efficient merging using pointers, making it more suitable for linked lists. Additionally, merge sort has a guaranteed O(n log n) time complexity, whereas quicksort has a worst-case O(n²) time complexity, which is less desirable for linked lists. Safe.
